l: AudioPhysx — audio that reacts to the world
p: A MetaSound and Blueprint toolkit for responsive, carefully designed Unreal Engine audio. AudioPhysx brings together flexible sample players, physically inspired processing, propagation tools and control utilities so you can make sounds respond to distance, material, movement and gameplay events without duplicating the same large node graph everywhere.

The plugin is designed around an important distinction: the game provides what happened and where, while the audio graph decides which recording is appropriate and how it should sound. Sometimes the best solution is a believable physical approximation; sometimes it is a deliberate, well-authored variation of a recording. The two approaches can work together.

The pages describe the newly uploaded UE 5.8.4 stereo source, including the RPM-enabled Start Loop End Player and the new Stereo to Mono converter. These are source-verified interfaces, not proof that every node has been compiled and tested in a packaged Shipping build. See compatibility before making release claims.

Playback tools handle the details that become repetitive in ordinary graphs: non-identical one-shots, shuffle-bag history, fixed and random sequences, synchronized layers, physical-material routing and held actions with proper endings. For example, the Start Loop End Player can schedule overlapping gunshot variations from a real RPM value while preserving a release tail when the player stops firing.

Acoustic tools take meaningful data from the world and transform the sound rather than guessing geometry from audio samples. Material Transmission filters sound that passes through barriers; Acoustic Paths renders one world-selected route; Early Reflections adds a lightweight sense of local space; Source Directivity can make the front of a speaker sound different from its rear. Each tool has its own purpose and limitations, explained in its reference page.

Stereo is now a first-class signal path. The playback and stereo DSP nodes provide Out Left and Out Right, preserving genuine channel differences. If the final sound should become a mono point-source emitter, AP: Stereo to Mono performs an explicit fold-down. The format decision belongs to the sound designer rather than being forced by every intermediate node. Read the stereo guide.

l: How to get a convincing result
p: Start with good source recordings and one clear goal. Choose a player that solves the required event timing, then add only processing that supplies a distinct audible benefit. A distance-based selection, a Doppler effect and a wall-transmission filter are three different tools; none automatically fixes an inaccurate listener position or a poorly edited Wave Asset. AudioPhysx aims to make these decisions approachable without pretending that every source must use every processor.

For a first exercise, follow your first MetaSound. If you already know MetaSounds, go straight to the node library. You can also browse examples or check troubleshooting when an installed graph does not behave as expected.

The fastest way to understand AudioPhysx is to make one sound work end to end before building a complicated acoustic system. You can begin with an ordinary imported recording, one trigger and a stereo MetaSound Source. Once the basic signal flows correctly, it becomes much easier to understand why a material-aware player, propagation processor or world-query component is useful.

This documentation uses the current stereo C++ source as its contract. An older MetaSound graph may still have Out Mono pins from a previous version of the plugin; those assets should be backed up and migrated deliberately rather than resaved as soon as Unreal refreshes their nodes.

Begin with installation. Confirm that the AudioPhysx plugin loads and the node categories appear in the MetaSound editor. Then read requirements and terminology for the difference between Wave Assets, audio buffers, control values and triggers. These distinctions prevent many silent-graph problems later.

Build your first MetaSound. The tutorial uses Sequence Wave Player because it demonstrates how playback timing and completion work without needing gameplay path queries or project-wide acoustic settings. After that, the stereo routing guide explains how to keep Left and Right channels or fold them down to mono for appropriate 3D sources.

Add game integration when the sound needs it. The Blueprint section explains how to obtain the physical material from a hit, submit a projectile path, and query a selected acoustic route. These calculations are useful, but they should not be made prerequisites for a simple random or layered sound effect.
If something does not play, use the setup checklist and troubleshooting. It is usually faster to isolate one missing Wave Asset or trigger than to adjust ten unrelated DSP settings.

AudioPhysx is a native C++ plugin for Unreal Engine. The code reviewed for this edition targets UE 5.8.4 and includes the stereo conversion and RPM playback system. That establishes what the source is intended to build against; it does not prove that a final Fab distribution has passed testing in every target build configuration. For current support claims, consult the compatibility page.

You need a compatible Unreal project with MetaSounds enabled, the complete AudioPhysx plugin installed and some legal Wave Assets for the tutorials. More advanced systems require meaningful game data: a projectile path, an impact location, source-listener separation, a hit Physical Material or an acoustic barrier and portal setup. The audio nodes cannot invent those values from a waveform alone.

A Wave Asset is a reference to an imported recording. A Wave Asset Array stores several recordings for variation, selection or layering. The array itself is not an audio stream; a Wave Player decides what to do with its contents when an event arrives.

An audio buffer carries actual samples. With the current stereo AudioPhysx convention, you normally connect the Left audio channel to the Left input of the next processor, and Right to Right. The final MetaSound Source output format should match the signal you want to render. If you intentionally need one mono stream, Stereo to Mono makes that conversion explicit.

A Trigger represents a point in time: play, stop, release, reset or announce completion. Triggers are not audio signals. A Float, Boolean, Integer, String or Float Array is a control value; it can describe distance, acoustic loss, random probability or surface identity without being either an event or an audio channel.

Most Unreal world coordinates and many AudioPhysx distances are expressed in centimetres. Other pins are explicitly labelled metres (m), metres per second (m/s), milliseconds (ms), seconds (s), decibels (dB), hertz (Hz), kilopascals (kPa) or semitones (st). Use the unit printed on the pin, because there is no universal convention that all values in the plugin are metres.

For example, a projectile whose closest approach is 500 Unreal units away is usually 500 cm, or 5 m. Feeding the number 500 to the flyby player's Distance (m) would tell it the projectile passed half a kilometre away. Likewise, a pitch ratio from Doppler Ratio is not interchangeable with a semitone pitch input.
If an effect sounds unexpectedly late, quiet or bright, verify the values and units before changing the DSP. Errors in source data can be far more dramatic than errors in a filter setting.

AudioPhysx can be installed either as a finished, compatible Fab code plugin or from a complete source distribution. This guide describes both approaches, but the current documentation package does not contain or redistribute the paid plugin source. In particular, a ZIP containing only Source/ is not by itself a distributable Unreal plugin: the descriptor and any required build configuration still need to be present.

If you have the Fab package, follow the supported Unreal/Fab installation flow for a verified engine version. Open your project, go to Edit → Plugins and confirm that AudioPhysx is enabled. Restart the Editor when prompted. The exact Launcher/Fab steps should be checked with the final released package, as the commercial installation has not been independently tested during this documentation task.

If you have the source distribution, close Unreal Editor and disable Live Coding. Place the complete plugin directory—including AudioPhysx.uplugin and the Source folder—under YourProject/Plugins/AudioPhysx/. Regenerate project files if necessary, compile the Editor target with the appropriate toolchain, and reopen the project. Do not mix old and new implementations of a node: duplicate registration functions and stale generated headers can cause misleading linker or startup errors.

Check the result in a MetaSound Source. Create a stereo MetaSound Source and search for AP: Random Wave Player or AudioPhysx in the node palette. Confirm the Wave Player has Out Left and Out Right pins, and confirm that AP: Stereo to Mono is available in QoL. This is a useful sanity check that the current stereo build, rather than an older mono DLL, has loaded.

If the plugin appears in the Plugins window but nodes are unavailable, inspect the Editor startup log and the first meaningful build or MetaSound registration message. A successful checkbox state does not prove the module has loaded its native nodes correctly. If you need to clear old build outputs, close the Editor before removing generated Binaries and Intermediate for a clean source rebuild.

A major part of this update changes audio pins from mono to stereo. Back up existing MetaSound assets before refreshing or replacing their AudioPhysx nodes. When you first open an older asset, check every input and output connection rather than assuming Unreal automatically transforms a single mono connection into two independent stereo connections.

New graphs are simplest to author as stereo from the beginning. For world emitters that should remain mono, connect the player or final DSP stage to AP: Stereo to Mono immediately before the Source's mono output. Test the finished graph in the Editor, then in a packaged Development build before relying on it in shipping content.

This example builds an action sound with three stages: a short click, a mechanical movement and a final latch. You will trigger the entire action once, and the Sequence Wave Player will start each recording after the preceding one finishes. The goal is to understand the difference between event wiring, stereo audio wiring and completion without involving any world-based acoustic calculations.

Create a stereo MetaSound Source and import three Wave Assets that you can distinguish easily. They may be mono or stereo recordings, but the AudioPhysx player will expose two channel outputs in the graph. Add AP: Sequence Wave Player from AudioPhysx → Playback and expand the Wave slots to three entries. Put the recordings into those slots in the desired order. The timing comes from the duration of each recording, not from a separate list of manually typed delays.

Connect the Source's On Play trigger to the player's Play input. Connect the player's Out Left to the stereo Source Left output and Out Right to the Source Right output. With Loop Sequence disabled, you can connect the player's On Finished to the MetaSound Source completion trigger when this player is the last audible stage. If you later add Early Reflections or Acoustic Paths, completion should instead account for the tail generated by the downstream processor.

Press Preview. The result should sound like one structured action: click, movement, latch. Now swap the middle recording for a much longer file. The last stage should happen later automatically because the player waits for playback completion. This is why a sequence node can be more robust than scheduling every stage with a hard-coded number of milliseconds.

Try turning on Loop Sequence. The complete three-part action should repeat rather than ending after its final clip. Turn looping off again and press Stop while the middle recording is audible. The stop request cancels the sequence; it is not the same thing as completing the sequence naturally, so do not assume it will issue On Finished.

When you want the three stages to remain in order but use different recordings on each play, move to Random Sequence Wave Player. When the stages should overlap instead of waiting for completion, try Layered Wave Player. Both now output stereo, so the channel-wiring pattern stays familiar.

If you are building a sound that should be precisely located at a point in 3D space, the stereo routing guide explains when to keep both channels and when to convert the final result to mono before spatialization.

l: Stereo routing and deliberate mono conversion
p: AudioPhysx's current design is stereo throughout audio-bearing playback and processing, with a dedicated node for conversion to mono. This is useful because it avoids discarding information before the sound designer has decided whether that information matters. It is not a statement that stereo is always acoustically preferable for every source in a 3D game.

Most Wave Players expose Out Left and Out Right. Acoustic processors commonly expect In Left and In Right and expose Out Left and Out Right again. Their delay and filter histories are separate, so a stereo recording can travel through the chain without being summed into mono at the first stage. The world controls—distance, obstruction, material or speed—are often shared across both channels because they describe one source-to-listener relationship.

A basic full-stereo path might begin with AP: Random Wave Player, continue through AP: Material Transmission, and then feed a stereo MetaSound Source. Connect the player's Left output to the processor's Left input and Right to Right. The processor's Left and Right outputs then connect to the corresponding Source channels. If you accidentally connect the same channel to both inputs, you may hear duplicated mono rather than the original stereo recording.

This also means you can combine source design and processing more freely. A Layered Wave Player can mix a stereo mechanical texture with other recordings; Early Reflections can preserve independent channel history; Dynamic Propagation can delay each stereo channel without first summing them. The effects still have limits and shared physical controls, but stereo content is no longer discarded merely because the plugin's internal renderer has a mono output.

l: When mono is still the better result
p: A small object making a footstep, a gun muzzle report or a collision at a known world position often behaves conceptually as a point source. Unreal's spatializer may be better suited to positioning one mono signal in 3D than a wide stereo recording whose left/right cues were captured or designed for a different listening position. The correct choice depends on the type of sound, the project's spatialization settings and the listening test.

To downmix, place AP: Stereo to Mono after the last stereo processor. Connect Out Left to In Left and Out Right to In Right; then feed its Out Mono into a mono MetaSound output. The node uses a simple sample-by-sample average:

This keeps dual-mono content at the same level rather than summing it 6 dB hotter. It cannot preserve the original stereo field, and opposite-polarity material may cancel during the fold-down. Always audition an important effect in mono before shipping it—especially if you have layered stereo bass or strongly phase-shifted recordings.

If your MetaSound was authored with an older AudioPhysx version, back it up before opening it in the stereo build. Verify the installed module is actually the stereo version, inspect saved node pins, reconnect Left and Right audio paths, and change the MetaSound Source output format only when the finished sound design needs it. Mono-only graphs can use the converter rather than forcing the entire pipeline back to mono.

Do not treat trigger and Float nodes as part of this migration. AP: Doppler Ratio, AP: Float Smoother, AP: Trigger Probability, AP: Trigger Cooldown and AP: Distance Switch do not render audio samples, so their existing event/number pin contracts remain appropriate. AP: Stereo to Mono is the deliberate mono-output exception. Recompile the graph and check real stereo separation using a test recording with noticeably different Left and Right content.
Read the Stereo to Mono node reference for the exact pin names and limitations.

A MetaSound graph contains different kinds of wires because it describes both events and continuous sound. Play, Stop, Reset and On Finished are triggers that represent moments. Out Left, Out Right, In Left and In Right carry the audio sample buffers. A Float such as Distance (cm) or Impact Strength describes a changing control value but does not itself produce sound.

Confusing these responsibilities is a common reason for nodes that appear to work individually but produce silence inside a larger graph. For example, a Wave Player can receive Play and load a valid sample without any audible result if its audio outputs are not connected to the Source. Conversely, an acoustic processor can have both audio channels connected but remain in the wrong state if the required material, route or obstruction input never updates.

l: Stopping and finishing are different events
p: A sound may finish naturally after rendering its final sample, or it may be explicitly cancelled by gameplay. Many AudioPhysx players reserve On Finished for natural completion. For that reason, pressing Stop should not be assumed to fire the same trigger as the end of the recording. Stop Firing on Start Loop End has another meaning: it requests the release phase and allows the ending to play.

Downstream processors introduce another consideration. A Wave Player may finish its original recording while Acoustic Paths is still delivering delayed samples or Early Reflections still has audible taps. In such a graph, the processor's Source Finished input can receive the player's completion signal, and the processor's own On Finished can indicate when the extended audible tail is complete. Ending the MetaSound Source too early cuts off that processing.

When routing the current stereo nodes, move each channel through the intended Left and Right path. The two channels carry separate audio buffer data; duplicating the Left buffer into both inputs is not equivalent to preserving a stereo recording. When you intentionally choose a mono Source, make the fold-down explicit with Stereo to Mono rather than relying on ambiguous routing or connecting a stereo pin into a mono-only input.

Some nodes have expandable pin groups for waves, steps or distance bands. These are part of the authored graph layout. Surface Wave Player can additionally generate pins from project settings. If an interface changes, check the actual pins and connections before saving migrated assets.

Most silent or incorrect AudioPhysx graphs can be diagnosed by working from the simplest part of the chain outward. First make sure a known-good Wave Asset plays through a basic stereo Source with the correct Out Left and Out Right wiring. Only then connect random selection, material routing, time delay or a world acoustic parameter. This separates an asset/import problem from a source-graph problem and from an acoustic-world problem.

When audio is silent, check that the correct start trigger actually reaches the node, that the relevant recording arrays contain playable assets, and that you have connected the outputs to an active MetaSound Source. For players that can reject a request, inspect On Rejected or an index output before assuming Unreal audio itself is failing.

When timing is wrong, distinguish a completion-driven sequence from RPM scheduling. Sequence Wave Player advances only when the current recording finishes. Start Loop End with positive RPM starts middle shots by a fixed interval and needs Stop Firing to enter the release phase. An extra Distance Delay or Acoustic Paths stage can delay the audible output even after the original playback has begun.

When world-driven sound is wrong, print the source-listener distance, physical material, obstruction result or selected acoustic route. Check units carefully: centimetres, metres and metres per second are used for different controls. A perfectly functioning filter cannot make an incorrect material path or invalid world trace meaningful.

Before shipping, test the exact plugin package in a clean project and compare Editor preview with packaged Development and Shipping audio. Include stereo and mono recordings, empty arrays, rapid retriggering and more than one simultaneously active sound. A clean Editor build is important, but it does not prove all runtime platform behaviour.

The current native source contains 24 nodes. They are divided by the job they perform rather than the feature that first inspired them: ten Wave Players for selecting recordings and scheduling playback, five acoustic processors for changing the character of audio, four propagation-related tools (one of which emits only a control value), and five QoL utilities including the new stereo-to-mono converter.

Understanding the difference between these groups is important. A playback node needs an event and usually some Wave Assets. A DSP processor needs an existing audio stream and physical or authored parameters. A control utility may have no audio pins at all because it decides which event passes or what number to use elsewhere. The pages are written to make those responsibilities clear before listing pin names.

The four categories expand directly in the left sidebar. Select a node to open its full explanation, five-step setup guide, stereo routing instructions, and expandable pin reference. There are no separate category-note pages to click through.

Playback handles Wave Asset playback, variation and timing. Start with Random Wave Player for one-shot variation, Random Sequence for multi-stage events, or Start Loop End for RPM-controlled firing and held actions.

Acoustics changes the character of an existing sound using world information or authored controls. Try Material Transmission to create a blocked-sound effect, or Acoustic Paths for a selected path's delay and frequency-band losses.
Propagation concerns travel time, source movement and absorption through air. Distance Delay works with latched travel-time delays; Dynamic Propagation responds to moving sources.
QoL streamlines control logic and conversion. Trigger Cooldown limits rapid events, Float Smoother softens parameter changes, and Stereo to Mono folds stereo down for a mono signal path.

l: How to read the reference pages
p: Each node begins with a practical explanation of the problem it solves. You will then find a more detailed discussion of what the node does to the sound or to the event flow, a real game-audio example, setup guidance and the risks worth testing. The complete pin descriptions are still present in an expandable Exact input and output pins section. They are extracted from the current C++ declarations, so you do not have to trust an older screenshot for the correct pin names.

The stereo convention is consistent across the audio processors: the input is typically In Left and In Right, and the output is Out Left and Out Right. Wave Players generally supply Out Left and Out Right. Control-only nodes are not artificially given audio channels. AP: Stereo to Mono deliberately outputs Out Mono because that is the point of the converter. If you are migrating an older MetaSound, see stereo routing and migration before saving the revised graph.
Want a complete walkthrough? Build your first MetaSound, then expand any node category in the sidebar. Every node has a dedicated five-step guide.

l: Playback: what should play, and when?
p: A convincing sound library needs more than a folder of recordings. It needs a clear decision about when an event begins, whether recordings overlap, how a variation is chosen, and when the audible result should actually end. AudioPhysx provides several players because these are genuinely different problems: an explosion can use a single variation, a machine may have a fixed mechanical sequence, and an automatic rifle needs a repeatable event cadence independent of individual recording duration.

For one-shot variation, start with Random Wave Player. It can choose a take whenever the game sends an event and allow limited overlap. If repeated events reveal the same recordings too often, Shuffle-Bag Wave Player adds selection history. Both produce stereo audio but do not decide the gameplay timing of the input trigger.

For structured actions, use Sequence Wave Player when every stage should play one specific recording, or Random Sequence Wave Player when each stage can select one of several variations. These wait for the current recording to finish. Layered Wave Player instead combines several recordings at once, with optional per-layer delays, gain and pitch. That difference between sequential and simultaneous audio is fundamental to how the sound will feel.

For held or context-dependent actions, Start Loop End Player manages an introduction, repeated middle and released ending. It now supports RPM-timed overlapping middle shots. Distance Wave Player chooses a recorded perspective using distance. PhysMat Wave Player and Surface Wave Player choose content from material identity, while Flyby Wave Player plays near-miss whizzes and optional cracks using data supplied by the flyby subsystem.

All ten Wave Players now expose Out Left and Out Right. That is a capability, not an instruction to make every source a wide stereo emitter. A localized footstep or weapon report may be better downmixed before 3D positioning, whereas a designed ambience or layered interface effect might benefit from keeping stereo intact. The stereo routing guide covers both cases.

A reliable starting point for any event that should sound familiar without replaying precisely the same recording every time.

The Random Wave Player takes a collection of Wave Assets and makes a selection whenever Play is triggered. Once the selection is accepted, that recording plays through the node's stereo output. Unlike a graph built from separate random-number, asset-switch and Wave Player elements, selection and concurrent playback are handled together. The node also exposes whether a requested start was rejected, which is useful when you are debugging empty arrays or reaching a voice limit.

Stereo matters particularly if the source recording contains actual left/right differences. The player now mixes its active voices into independent Out Left and Out Right buffers, rather than collapsing recordings to a single channel. If this is a tightly positioned 3D footstep, you may still choose to downmix at the end of the graph; the point is that no early stage forces you to discard stereo material.

Consider a character handling a set of loose metal objects. You might have six recordings of a similar small impact, each with slightly different rhythm and resonance. Randomly choosing between them prevents a short repeated animation from sounding machine-generated. For a weapon or collision system, the same node can respond to closely spaced triggers while older recordings are still ringing out, up to the configured voice limit.

A collection of recordings should sound like a family. Random selection does not automatically equalize their loudness or remove poorly trimmed silence. Prepare the Wave Assets so the listener notices physical variation rather than inconsistent editing.

l: Build the sound — step by step
p: The setup below is deliberately small so you can hear what this node contributes before adding more systems. Create the sound in a fresh test MetaSound first, then copy the working graph into your game.

In the Content Browser, create a MetaSound Source with Stereo as its output format. Add AP: Random Wave Player from AudioPhysx. This simple graph tests selection and playback before adding any environmental processing.

Import at least three short recordings of the same event, such as mechanical clicks or impacts. Build a Wave Asset Array and connect it to Waves. Keep the takes at roughly comparable loudness so that random selection does not cause an unintended volume jump.
Connect the Source On Play trigger to Play. Leave Stop disconnected for this first one-shot test. Enable No Immediate Repeat when you have more than one valid recording.
Connect Out Left to the Source left output and Out Right to its right output. Set Max Voices conservatively; it controls how many triggered recordings can overlap.

Play the Source several times and check Selected Index if you are debugging which take was chosen. Rapidly retrigger to confirm your chosen voice limit is appropriate. On Rejected is a useful signal when nothing can play.

After the basic setup: Create a stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Random Wave Player. Supply several recordings to Waves, connect On Play or your own event to Play, and connect Out Left and Out Right to the corresponding Source outputs. Begin with a modest Max Voices setting, trigger the node repeatedly, and listen for overlap. If the Source is intentionally mono, route the two outputs into AP: Stereo to Mono first.

When No Immediate Repeat is enabled, the node attempts to avoid selecting the previous recording when there is more than one valid option. Selected Index makes it easy to confirm that selection is working even when the recordings happen to sound similar.

Pitch Shift (st) alters playback pitch in semitones; positive values are higher, negative values lower. This is a playback-rate-style change, so consider how it affects perceived duration and naturalness. Max Voices limits how many recordings may exist simultaneously. On Finished indicates natural completion of the final active voice, whereas On Rejected identifies an unsuccessful start request rather than playing a replacement silence. These are event outputs, not audio buffers.

Practical limitations. For performance, avoid setting voice capacity arbitrarily high on effects triggered dozens of times per frame. More active voices mean more decoding and mixing work. Audition realistic bursts in a packaged Development build and verify that the sound still follows the gameplay event when the pool is busy. A single long ambient recording would generally be better served by a normal Unreal playback workflow than a constantly retriggered random one-shot player.
Related: Shuffle-Bag Wave Player if you want a selection history rather than an unrestricted random draw.

Variation selection that deliberately uses a bag of eligible recordings instead of always making an unrestricted random choice.

A shuffle bag is useful when ordinary randomness still sounds repetitive. In a small sound library, the same take can be selected several times in a row by chance. Here, each eligible entry participates in the current bag, and Play draws from the remaining entries. When a cycle is exhausted, another bag can be constructed. Optional weights influence how the eligible entries participate in that selection process; they do not change the volume of the Wave Asset.

Playback remains fully stereo. Each accepted sound is mixed into Out Left and Out Right, so a recorded stereo rustle or environmental hit can retain its channel information. Selected Index and Bag Remaining provide useful feedback for diagnosing unexpected variation choices without listening for tiny differences between similar clips.

Imagine an NPC walking over a dry wooden floor. With a random player, it is possible to hear the same distinctive creak repeatedly. A bag approach distributes selection more deliberately across available takes. It can also work well for repeated mechanical clunks, short movement details and sets of similar destruction fragments.

Do not confuse this with timing or sequencing. A shuffle bag determines which recording to play next. Your animation, footsteps system or game event still determines when the next Play trigger arrives.

l: Build the sound — step by step
p: The setup below is deliberately small so you can hear what this node contributes before adding more systems. Create the sound in a fresh test MetaSound first, then copy the working graph into your game.
Create a Stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Shuffle-Bag Wave Player. Use several distinct recordings of the same event so the changing choices are easy to hear.
Fill Waves with at least four takes. Leave Weights empty for the simplest test, or provide one non-negative weight per recording; a weight of zero excludes that entry.
Connect Source On Play to the player Play. Optionally expose a separate trigger for Reset Bag so you can deliberately restart its selection cycle.
Connect Out Left and Out Right to the corresponding outputs of the MetaSound. Watch Selected Index and Bag Remaining if you need to confirm the selection sequence.

Trigger the graph repeatedly and listen for distributed choices. Try Seed with a known nonzero value to reproduce a sequence while debugging. Increase Max Voices only if simultaneous playback is actually required.

After the basic setup: Create a Wave Asset Array with your variations, then connect it to Waves. Weights is optional; its entries correspond by index to the Wave Assets, so keep the arrays aligned when you add or remove a recording. Connect the trigger and both stereo outputs in the same way as any other player. Trigger through a complete cycle and observe the remaining count to understand the node's behaviour.

Use Reset Bag when you intentionally want to abandon the current selection history, such as after moving to a completely different interaction context. Resetting the bag does not automatically stop existing voices, so the sound that is already audible need not be cut off.

Seed controls reproducibility. A fixed, nonzero seed is useful when testing the same sequence repeatedly; the source defines zero as a request for a new random seed. Pitch Shift (st) and Gain (dB) affect newly started voices, not the weights. Max Voices controls simultaneous playback. Rejected selections are reported through On Rejected when there is no playable eligible choice or available voice.

Practical limitations. This node is not a content-quality substitute: obviously different loudness or inconsistent noise floors can reveal the individual recording choices. Very high weights may cause the distribution to feel less even than expected, and zero-weight entries are intentionally ineligible. Check selection in a realistic playback run rather than assuming a handful of preview clicks establishes the distribution.
Related: Random Wave Player when you do not need bag history.
Bag Remaining — Integer. Number of unplayed entries left in the current bag.
Gain (dB) — Float. Gain for newly started voices, -96 to +12 dB.

Play several recordings one after another, using the recordings themselves to determine when each step should advance.

The Sequence Wave Player is a completion-driven sound arranger. It exposes an expandable set of individual Wave inputs, and the node works through them in their authored order. When one playable recording finishes, the next begins. This is fundamentally different from adding a trigger delay of a fixed number of milliseconds: changing a recording's duration does not require you to maintain a parallel list of manual delays.

The source now supplies two audio outputs. If your click, motor and release recordings were authored in stereo, their left/right differences remain available across the entire sequence. A fixed sequence is not a multi-layer mixer; the intention is that one ordered element follows another.

A useful example is a mechanical lock: a short button press, the mechanical motor opening the mechanism, then a final latch sound. The game only issues one start event. The player takes care of the boundaries between the elements, making it easier to replace a middle recording without breaking the timing of the last.

This is also a good beginner node because it demonstrates the distinction between a trigger and an audio buffer. Play begins the operation, while Out Left and Out Right carry continuous audio until the sequence ends.

l: Build the sound — step by step
p: The setup below is deliberately small so you can hear what this node contributes before adding more systems. Create the sound in a fresh test MetaSound first, then copy the working graph into your game.
Create a Stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Sequence Wave Player. Choose three short recordings forming a clear action, such as a click, a mechanical movement and a final clunk.
Expand the node’s Wave group to three Wave inputs. Assign one Wave Asset to each in playback order; this node expects individual assets rather than one array holding every stage.
Connect the Source On Play to the node Play. Leave Loop Sequence unchecked for the initial test; otherwise the action will repeat instead of naturally completing.
Connect Out Left and Out Right to the Source outputs. If this is the last processor, connect node On Finished to the Source completion input so it ends after the final stage.

Audition once, then replace the middle recording with a longer clip. The third recording should start only after the new middle clip ends. Test Stop separately to distinguish cancellation from natural completion.

After the basic setup: In a stereo MetaSound Source, add the node and expand the sequence group to reveal the number of Wave Asset slots you need. Assign each recording in the order you want it played, then connect the Source's On Play to Play. Connect the two stereo outputs to the respective Source channels. With Loop Sequence disabled, connect On Finished to the Source completion pin when no other processor needs to play a tail.

Audition with a deliberately longer recording in the middle and verify that the third sound begins after it, not at a fixed elapsed time. Play again restarts the sequence; Stop explicitly cancels playback without claiming natural completion.

Loop Sequence repeats the complete set after the last playable entry. That can make sense for a repetitive machine pattern, but it is not a held gun trigger or a release phase. On Finished is meaningful for a non-looping pass after the final recording has naturally ended. For sustained gunfire with a stop-triggered outro, prefer the specialized Start Loop End Player.

Practical limitations. This node does not randomly choose the contents of its steps: the selected Wave Asset for each slot is fixed in the graph. If you need an ordered action with a different take at each phase, use Random Sequence. If recordings must overlap rather than follow completion, use Layered Wave Player. These distinctions matter more for believable sound design than the number of pins on the nodes.
Related: Random Sequence Wave Player for randomized variation within each step.

A predictable beginning, middle and end—but with fresh recording choices inside every stage.

Random Sequence combines two ideas: ordered playback and random variation. Each expandable step receives a Wave Asset Array, not one Wave Asset. When the player reaches a step, it selects a playable member of that array, plays it to completion, and then advances to the next step. The number of stages and the recordings inside each stage are two separate design decisions.

This lets you build recognizably structured events without every repetition sounding identical. Because the outputs are now Out Left and Out Right, both the chosen recording and the change from one stage to another can retain genuine stereo content. The selection is made when a stage begins; it is not a continuous shuffle of a playing recording.

Consider opening a sci-fi container. You always want an authorization beep, a motor action and a seal release, but you recorded several different beeps, motor passes and sealing noises. Three ordered arrays give you the same functional sequence every time while avoiding the exact same combination of sounds on every interaction.

This works particularly well for repeated gameplay interactions where the timing depends on the actual recordings. You do not need to enter the motor duration anywhere in the graph: the next phase follows playback completion.

Practical limitations. Make sure each array contains recordings belonging to the same functional stage. A long release sample accidentally placed in the middle-stage array will delay the final stage by its full length. Likewise, the node cannot automatically synchronize a mechanically meaningful animation; it schedules audio by audio completion, so gameplay effects that must coincide with particular subevents may still require event markers or explicit triggers.

Combine several recordings into a single composite sound while controlling the level, pitch and onset of each layer.

Many complex game sounds are deliberately built from layers: a sharp transient that establishes the attack, a low-frequency body that provides weight, and a mechanical or environmental texture that identifies the object. Layered Wave Player starts those recordings as one stack and mixes them into stereo output. Each layer has its own recording, optional gain, optional pitch offset and optional start delay.

The controls use aligned arrays: the value at index 2 in Layer Gains (dB) belongs to the Wave Asset at index 2 in Layer Waves. Missing optional array values default to the documented neutral values. Separate left/right audio buffers mean layered stereo recordings remain stereo rather than being mixed into a single common channel.

Think of an energy weapon: a short bright crack, a low synthesized pulse and a delayed resonance tail. Rather than pre-rendering every possible combination, you can author three independent recordings and control their balance in the MetaSound. The third layer may begin a few milliseconds later to make the source feel heavier without pretending that every recorded element started at the exact same instant.
The same approach is useful for mechanical impacts, doors, or cinematic effects, although it should not be applied to every tiny event simply because layering is available.

p: The setup below is deliberately small so you can hear what this node contributes before adding more systems. Create the sound in a fresh test MetaSound first, then copy the working graph into your game.
Make a Stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Layered Wave Player. Choose recordings that belong to one event, such as a gunshot transient, low-frequency body and mechanical click.
Put the recordings into Layer Waves in the order you want to address them. For a first test, use three layers, not the maximum eight, so the sound is easy to judge.

Optionally create Layer Gains (dB), Layer Pitch (st) and Layer Delays (ms) Float Arrays. Their entries line up by index with Layer Waves: index 0 controls the first recording, index 1 the second, and so on.
Connect Source On Play to Play, then wire Out Left and Out Right to the stereo outputs. Set Max Voices high enough for every layer in one triggered stack, but do not use a larger pool than necessary.
Audition the combined effect and adjust gain/delay until the layers form one coherent event. Use Active Layers and On Rejected to investigate capacity issues; summing multiple loud layers can clip.

After the basic setup: Populate Layer Waves in a clear order and, if needed, add matching entries to Layer Gains (dB), Layer Pitch (st) and Layer Delays (ms). The current implementation allows up to eight configured layers. Trigger Play once and connect Out Left / Out Right to the Source. Start with zero gain offsets and zero delays so you can hear the natural edit points, then adjust one layer at a time.

The node treats one stack as a coordinated event. If it cannot reserve sufficient voices for an eligible stack, it can reject the request rather than partially starting only some layers. Active Layers helps diagnose how much of the voice budget is currently occupied.

Layer Gains (dB) are per-layer trims, not master volume. Layer Pitch (st) uses semitone offsets, and Layer Delays (ms) shifts the start time of each layer by up to the configured supported range. Max Voices is the total voice budget across currently playing stacks, not the number of possible layer slots. On Rejected reports a stack that could not start; On Finished indicates natural completion after the final active layer.

Practical limitations. Stereo layering creates more opportunities for phase and loudness problems. Two low-frequency recordings with different timing may reinforce or cancel each other unpredictably. Use realistic game volumes, inspect peaks, and try the final output both in stereo and downmixed to mono, particularly if the effect will be spatialized as a single point in the world.
Related: Stereo to Mono when the finished effect must feed a mono Source.

One sound can have a meaningful start, a repeating body, and a release that only plays when the action ends.

Start Loop End is built around the lifecycle of a sustained action. Its three Wave Asset Arrays provide possible start, middle, and end recordings. A start trigger first plays an introductory variation when one is available, then enters the middle phase. When Stop Firing arrives, the node stops scheduling new middle events and transitions into a final recording. This separation is essential for weapons, continuous tools and machines that should not abruptly stop when a button is released.

The RPM input changes how the middle phase behaves. With RPM = 0, the next middle recording starts after the last one has finished—the older sequential mode. With positive RPM, new middle recordings are scheduled according to rounds per minute, even if older middle recordings are still audible. The current code uses a bounded pool of twelve middle voices for overlap. Both channels of each chosen recording are mixed to Out Left and Out Right.

For automatic gunfire, try a brief attack recording, several main shot variations, and one or more release recordings. At 600 RPM, the intended interval between middle-shot starts is 100 milliseconds. A recording that lasts 250 milliseconds can therefore overlap subsequent shots. That is fundamentally different from cutting each clip to 100 milliseconds or speeding it up to fit the firing cadence.
The same system can also describe a held industrial tool. Set RPM to zero for a completion-based repeating middle, and use an authentic winding-down recording when the player releases the control.

p: The setup below is deliberately small so you can hear what this node contributes before adding more systems. Create the sound in a fresh test MetaSound first, then copy the working graph into your game.
Create a Stereo MetaSound Source and add AP: Start Loop End Player. Prepare recordings for the beginning of an action, its repeating middle, and its ending.

Fill Start Waves with optional intro recordings, Loop Waves with repeatable middle variations, and End Waves with release or tail sounds. For a rifle, the middle array contains the main shot variations.
Connect an input or gameplay event representing button pressed to Start Firing. Connect the button released event to Stop Firing. The node needs the release event to exit the held playback state.

Set RPM = 600 to schedule a new middle shot about every 100 ms once the intro finishes. Choose Immediate Release for a quick fade into the ending; otherwise active middle recordings finish before the outro.

Connect Out Left and Out Right to the stereo Source. Use On Finished for the completion of the released sound. Test rapidly stopping and restarting, then try RPM = 0 to hear the original completion-driven middle loop.

After the basic setup: Add the node to a stereo Source, provide Start Waves, Loop Waves and End Waves, and connect the weapon's pressed event to Start Firing. Connect the release event to Stop Firing; sending only the start event leaves the player in its sustained state. Connect the left and right outputs to the stereo Source, or downmix deliberately for a mono spatialized Source. Begin with 600 RPM and test how recorded clip duration changes the overlap.

Toggle Immediate Release while holding and releasing the action. With it enabled, currently active waves fade quickly and the end begins promptly. With it disabled, active recordings finish before the ending starts. On Finished is intended to signal completion of the released sequence, not to fire after each middle shot.

RPM = 0 preserves sequential middle playback. A positive value is bounded by the implementation's supported range of 60–2400 RPM. This controls the start intervals, not the source playback speed. The code maintains a maximum of twelve middle voices; when every voice is occupied, a new scheduled shot is skipped instead of abruptly cutting another. Immediate Release changes release semantics but does not make existing recordings disappear retroactively unless the fade path is selected.

Practical limitations. Test starting and stopping in the middle of the introduction, releasing while several middle shots overlap, and retriggering while the ending is audible. Also test empty arrays and a long middle recording at high RPM to expose voice saturation. This is a playback scheduler, not a ballistic or weapons-logic system: gameplay still decides exactly when shots happen and when to send the release trigger.

Choose a different recorded perspective at different distances, rather than relying on volume attenuation alone.

A gunshot ten metres away often needs different recorded content from one heard several hundred metres away. Distance Wave Player evaluates Distance (cm) when Play arrives and uses the configured distance range to select a recording. Each expandable range has a start distance, a Wave Asset Array, and a volume setting. This lets the same gameplay event choose a near, medium or far recording without building a separate switch network for each sound.

The decision is made when playback starts. The player is not designed to continuously crossfade a recording that has already begun as the listener crosses a range boundary. Once accepted, the selected sound plays with its latched range gain and retains two audio output channels.

A useful application is a rifle report with separate close mechanical detail and distant tails. At short range, you may emphasize the muzzle report; farther away, you may want the environmental tail and less close-microphone detail. The node selects the appropriate authored material when the sound fires, while Unreal attenuation can continue to manage overall distance level and source spatialization.
For a repeatable test, move the listener between two fixed distances and trigger the sound at each location. You should hear a different recording pool, not just a quieter version of the same one.

Connect On Play to Play and wire Out Left/Out Right to the Source outputs. If needed, set Max Voices and No Immediate Repeat to handle repeated events.

Set a close distance and trigger the sound, then try a far distance and trigger again. The selected sample should change according to the band. A change in distance does not automatically crossfade a recording already playing.

After the basic setup: Configure the dynamic distance ranges in ascending order of Start Distance (cm), then assign one or more recordings to each Waves array. Supply the listener-source separation to Distance (cm) and connect Play and the two stereo outputs. Set Max Distance (cm) deliberately; it is a hard cutoff evaluated when a new sound is requested, not an automatic fade applied to all currently playing voices.
Use No Immediate Repeat when several takes exist in a range. Trigger the player in a test level with a known numerical distance before integrating any automatic listener-distance calculation.

Volume in a range is a linear playback multiplier, not a decibel value. This matters when you match the apparent loudness of near and far captures. Max Voices determines permitted overlap, and On Finished fires when the final naturally playing voice completes. There is no inherent acoustic air-absorption or Doppler calculation in the selection logic; those are separate responsibilities.

Practical limitations. Keep the boundaries meaningful and avoid excessive ranges with recordings that are nearly identical. A hard change between badly matched pools can be obvious during repeated action at a range boundary. Source location and built-in Unreal attenuation still need to be configured correctly. For simple trigger branching without an integrated Wave Player, Distance Switch is a lighter control-flow tool.

Choose impact or interaction recordings using the exact Physical Material asset involved in the event.

Physical Materials can distinguish surfaces more precisely than a broad surface category. PhysMat Wave Player accepts a string path identifying the hit Physical Material and compares it to the configured route entries. When it finds a match, it selects from the associated Wave Asset Array; otherwise, it can use Default Waves. This is a sound-selection mechanism, not a world trace. Your gameplay or Blueprint system is responsible for obtaining the correct hit result and material identity.

The node now renders its selected recording in stereo. That means a stereo-captured surface impact can preserve channel differences through the player, even if you later choose to downmix it for a mono, spatialized world emitter.

Suppose two metal objects share the game's general metal category: a thin sheet and a heavy steel plate. You may want a lightweight, bright rattle for the sheet and a dense ringing impact for the plate. Assign those objects different Physical Materials, configure the paths, and let the player select a different pool for each.

A reasonable fallback is important in a large project. New levels and assets may introduce materials that were never explicitly mapped; supplying Default Waves prevents those legitimate interactions from becoming silent.

Use Unreal physical surface types to select footstep, impact or interaction variations through one MetaSound player.

Surface Wave Player uses the integer value of EPhysicalSurface supplied through Hit Surface Type. Configured AudioPhysx routes determine which surface-specific Wave Asset Array should be used, with Default Waves available for unmatched values. This is especially useful when the game already classifies surfaces into a manageable set such as grass, concrete, gravel and metal.

The surface-specific pins are generated from configuration, rather than being identical in every possible project. That reduces pointless pins when only a few surfaces are used, but it creates an authoring responsibility: if route configuration changes, inspect the saved MetaSound graph to ensure its dynamic input layout still matches the intended assets.

In a footstep system, the animation usually defines the exact timing of the step and the gameplay trace identifies the ground material. Surface Wave Player uses that supplied value to choose a recording pool. It does not perform the character's foot trace or decide how often footsteps should occur.

With stereo output, a designer can preserve deliberately stereo footstep recordings through the graph. For a single, precisely positioned footstep in the world, downmixing to mono just before the Source output may still be the better spatial choice.

Turn a near-miss calculation into an audible projectile whizz, with an optional ballistic-crack layer.

Flyby Wave Player handles playback, while a separate Blueprint/world subsystem evaluates the projectile path. The node chooses a whizz recording from Whizz Waves, and can additionally select a Crack Waves recording when the supplied shock condition requests it. Distance (m), Speed (m/s), Intensity, Speed of Sound (m/s) and Shock describe the result of the path calculation rather than controlling a generic random one-shot.

The chosen recordings render into independent Left and Right output channels. The final Source can still be spatialized by Unreal, and the game-side subsystem can schedule the sound near the closest approach. This division keeps world geometry and projectile event logic off MetaSound's real-time audio thread.

A fast projectile passing just beside the listener should sound noticeably different from one passing tens of metres away. A supersonic close pass may call for both a whizz and a sharp crack, while a slow object or a path whose shock cone does not reach the listener should not automatically create that same crack. The recordings supply the cinematic character; the gameplay calculation supplies the conditions under which they should play.
This is useful with hitscan weapons as well as moving projectiles submitting successive path segments. You do not have to build a custom Chaos rigid-body simulation merely to evaluate a near miss.

First audition with manually supplied values, then call AP: Play Projectile Flyby from gameplay using a path start, path end, speed in metres per second and audible radius in metres. The Boolean acceptance result tells you whether the event was scheduled, not necessarily whether audio has reached the listener yet.

Shock is an explicit 0/1-style request for the crack layer; it is not a generic measure of volume. Distance (m) is measured in metres even though Unreal world locations are commonly centimetres. Intensity is a normalized strength control. The player exposes On Rejected for unavailable content and On Finished for natural completion; Stop cancels immediately without the normal finish event.

Practical limitations. The current system uses simplified constant-speed path and acoustic timing. It should not be marketed as an exact ballistic shock-wave simulation or as a continuous physically traced sound source. Always test duplicate suppression on moving projectiles, sensible near-miss thresholds and the audio Source's spatialization policy with the final packaged build.

l: Playback: what should play, and when?
p: A convincing sound library needs more than a folder of recordings. It needs a clear decision about when an event begins, whether recordings overlap, how a variation is chosen, and when the audible result should actually end. AudioPhysx provides several players because these are genuinely different problems: an explosion can use a single variation, a machine may have a fixed mechanical sequence, and an automatic rifle needs a repeatable event cadence independent of individual recording duration.

For one-shot variation, start with Random Wave Player. It can choose a take whenever the game sends an event and allow limited overlap. If repeated events reveal the same recordings too often, Shuffle-Bag Wave Player adds selection history. Both produce stereo audio but do not decide the gameplay timing of the input trigger.

For structured actions, use Sequence Wave Player when every stage should play one specific recording, or Random Sequence Wave Player when each stage can select one of several variations. These wait for the current recording to finish. Layered Wave Player instead combines several recordings at once, with optional per-layer delays, gain and pitch. That difference between sequential and simultaneous audio is fundamental to how the sound will feel.

For held or context-dependent actions, Start Loop End Player manages an introduction, repeated middle and released ending. It now supports RPM-timed overlapping middle shots. Distance Wave Player chooses a recorded perspective using distance. PhysMat Wave Player and Surface Wave Player choose content from material identity, while Flyby Wave Player plays near-miss whizzes and optional cracks using data supplied by the flyby subsystem.

All ten Wave Players now expose Out Left and Out Right. That is a capability, not an instruction to make every source a wide stereo emitter. A localized footstep or weapon report may be better downmixed before 3D positioning, whereas a designed ambience or layered interface effect might benefit from keeping stereo intact. The stereo routing guide covers both cases.

l: Acoustics: why does a place change the sound?
p: A recording played through a loudspeaker should not sound identical in every physical situation. It may be blocked by a door, travel around an opening, lose high-frequency detail when the source faces away, or produce an initial set of room reflections. AudioPhysx separates these phenomena into focused processing nodes so you can build only the behaviour needed by a particular sound.

Material Transmission uses an externally supplied obstruction state and material losses to colour a sound through a barrier. Acoustic Paths takes a world-selected route and applies its delay plus low/mid/high frequency losses. The two nodes can sound similar in some situations, but one is an authored material-filter approach and the other is a route-driven processor. Applying both at full strength without a reason can make a source much darker than intended.

Early Reflections is meant to suggest the first short returns from nearby surfaces. It is not the same as pathing through a doorway and is not a complete acoustic room solve. Source Directivity changes the signal with the listener-relative angle, allowing a front-facing emitter to sound more present than when heard from behind. Impact Dynamics shapes transients according to an externally supplied impact strength; it is a DSP stage, not a collision detector.

Every one of these processors now accepts Left and Right audio inputs and emits Left and Right audio outputs. The world/material controls remain shared where that makes physical sense, while channel-specific filter or delay history is kept separate. That lets an effect treat stereo content without reducing it prematurely to one channel. If you later want a mono positional emitter, convert at the end of the relevant chain.

The realism comes from the input data as much as the signal processing. Before adjusting the filter or reflection wetness, verify that the game is sending the correct obstruction, angle, material or impact strength. Blueprint acoustic integration describes where these values come from.

Render the single acoustic route selected by the world solver, including travel delay and frequency-dependent loss, without creating duplicate sound copies.

The Acoustic Paths node receives stereo audio and a compact Selected Route Float Array. That array contains four values in a strict order: delay in milliseconds, low-band loss in decibels, mid-band loss, and high-band loss. It is normally supplied by the AudioPhysx game-thread path system through AP.AcousticRoute.Selected. The solver decides which route is appropriate; this MetaSound node turns that selected route into audible delay and spectral reduction.

The distinction between direct and around-obstacle sound matters. When an opening provides a better path, the system can prefer that route over heavily transmitted sound through a barrier. The current audio node applies one selected route rather than playing two simultaneous copies of the source. Separate channel histories preserve differences between Left and Right while the same route data controls their acoustic treatment.

Imagine a radio playing behind a heavy wall with an open doorway nearby. A direct line to the listener might intersect the wall and require substantial high-frequency loss, while the route through the doorway might travel farther but preserve more clarity. Rather than choosing based solely on the shortest distance, an acoustic routing system can compare available route losses and select the preferred listening result.

This approach is particularly effective when the sound designer wants perceptual plausibility without asking the audio renderer to perform geometry queries. The world solver works on a scheduled game-thread budget; the MetaSound processor simply receives already calculated values.

Begin by testing a clear route with near-zero loss and delay, then feed deliberately larger high-band loss and a controlled delay. Give an obstructed sound a believable tonal change rather than making it merely quieter.

Sound transmitted through a door, wall or panel often loses more high-frequency detail than low-frequency weight. Material Transmission takes stereo audio and an externally supplied Obstructed Boolean, then applies a frequency-shaped loss model whose low/high loss values describe the material. Thickness and reference thickness provide a way to scale that treatment with the geometry represented by your game data.

The node is a DSP processor, not a raycaster. It cannot know that a wall exists unless a Blueprint, component or world path calculation supplies the obstruction state. Left and Right inputs are processed with separate filter histories so differences in a stereo recording are not forcibly collapsed. The broad obstruction amount, however, is controlled by the same material inputs for both channels.

Try a metal door between the player and a nearby machine. The unobstructed version should contain clear clicks and bright mechanical texture. When the door closes, a filtered version might retain some low rumble but lose much of the sharp top end. A small amount of leakage can preserve an audible sense that the machine is still present, especially if you have deliberately designed a thin or imperfect barrier.

This sounds more convincing than a volume-only change because the tonal balance communicates the idea of an intervening object. It can also communicate the quality of the material: a lighter partition and a heavy sealed wall should not have identical transmitted spectra.

Make the source sound different when the listener stands in front of it, beside it, or behind it.

Many sound sources radiate unevenly. A voice tends to carry more clarity in front of the speaker, while the rear of a device may attenuate sharp detail without fully eliminating its low-frequency body. Source Directivity receives stereo audio and a listener-relative Angle (deg), then shapes the output according to the authored directivity strength, rear attenuation and frequency division.

The input angle must come from the game or another world-audio parameter system. The DSP node is not a position tracker, and it cannot deduce a source Actor's forward vector from the waveform. By retaining separate filter histories for Left and Right, the processing stage preserves stereo differences while applying a common source-orientation response.

Place a portable radio or loud mechanical generator in a test room. Walk around it in a circle with a steady recording playing. The front should have more presence while the rear sounds comparatively subdued. If you rotate the emitter itself, the apparent bright/dark pattern should rotate with it rather than being permanently aligned to the level.
This provides a useful layer of realism for sources with a meaningful forward-facing axis. It is less useful for a small spherical point source that should radiate almost equally in all directions.

Use one impact recording more expressively by changing its attack and colour according to how hard the impact was.

Impact Dynamics takes an existing stereo audio recording plus an Impact trigger and an Impact Strength control in the 0–1 range. It uses the strength to interpolate between soft and hard gain/filter settings, with an additional transient enhancement for stronger events. This can make a single usable asset feel gentler for a light contact and brighter or more aggressive for a forceful collision.

It does not detect a collision or compute collision impulse inside the audio thread. Your game, animation, trace or Blueprint helper decides that an impact occurred and provides a meaningful strength value. The node then shapes the audio. Both channels are processed independently, preserving the stereo source while applying the same intended impact strength.

Imagine a character dropping a small tool onto a wooden surface. A very light contact may need a soft, muted tap; a much stronger drop can need a brighter transient and greater level. Rather than importing dozens of almost identical strength variations, you can use a few recordings with dynamics that follow the gameplay's impact-strength signal.

This becomes particularly valuable for many small environmental interactions. It should still be driven by plausible events: setting the strength to 1 on every minor collision can make an otherwise natural scene sound exaggerated and exhausting.

Soft Gain and Hard Gain are linear gain controls, while the cutoff inputs are in hertz. Transient Boost adds attack emphasis, with Transient Time (ms) determining how long that emphasis lasts. A normalized strength represents an authored mapping from gameplay force, not a universal physical unit such as newtons.

A strong impact can consist of several physical stages—first contact, material resonance and secondary movement—so dynamics processing cannot replace all variation in source recordings. Use a good base sound, and consider Layered Wave Player or material-based selection when a change in physical material is more important than a change in force. Profile simultaneous impacts in a dense scene before raising every node's transient enhancement.

Add short, synthetic reflection taps that suggest nearby boundaries without running a full room simulation.

Early reflections are some of the first distinct returns you hear after a short sound strikes surfaces in a space. A hand clap in a small room has a different initial tail from the same clap outdoors. This node creates a compact group of synthetic delayed reflections from a room-size estimate, sound speed and damping settings, mixing them with the dry stereo signal.

The reflected channels have independent state. This matters because a stereo recording can contain meaningful differences that should survive an effect, even though the same approximate room settings are applied to both sides. The node is not tracing the precise room geometry or generating an impulse response from your level. It deliberately offers a fast, editable suggestion of near-field reflections.

Try a dry finger snap, short metal hit or rifle report. Increase the Wet Level gradually and listen for small delayed arrivals after the direct sound. A larger Room Size should suggest a broader spacing of early returns, while stronger HF Damping makes those returns less bright. The goal is to help locate a sound in an environment without creating a long, washed-out reverb tail.

If your game already uses a global late reverb, early reflections can complement it—provided the timing and balance are intentional. Two sets of strong reflections from separate systems can sound unnaturally busy.

l: Propagation: when sound takes time to reach us
p: Propagation concerns how a sound changes while travelling from its source to the listener. In the real world, an explosion heard at a great distance arrives after its flash, and a moving source can exhibit Doppler shift. In a game, these effects must be balanced against latency, memory and the fact that the level geometry and player motion may update suddenly rather than continuously.

Distance Delay captures a travel-time delay based on distance and sound speed. It works well for discrete events whose distance can be latched. Dynamic Propagation changes the delay continuously for a moving source and includes smoothing and jump handling to keep the audible result controlled. Both are stereo DSP nodes and maintain separate channel delay histories.

Doppler Ratio computes a pitch multiplier from relative radial motion. It does not output audio—there is no reason to manufacture left and right audio channels for a single numeric ratio. Use it when another playback stage needs a pitch control, and avoid applying it again to a sound whose Dynamic Propagation has already introduced Doppler-like movement.

Atmosphere Absorption adjusts high-frequency content according to travelled distance and environmental conditions. It is separate from a wall-transmission filter and separate from ordinary source volume attenuation. In some projects Unreal's own air absorption may already be active, so compare the complete chain before using both systems together.

These are physically motivated approximations, not guaranteed measurements of the acoustic field in your level. A reliable design uses the right units and limits processing to what the listener can actually perceive. The individual references discuss centimetres, metres per second and buffer capacities in detail.

Delay a sound by its estimated travel time across an authored source-to-listener distance.

Sound travels through air at a finite speed. The Distance Delay node converts Distance (cm) and Speed of Sound (m/s) into a delay and passes the stereo input through buffered output. Unlike a free-running moving-source simulation, it supports an explicit Relatch trigger: you can capture a new travel time for an event rather than continuously scrubbing the buffer as the source moves.

Both audio channels have their own delay history. This preserves a stereo recording's internal differences instead of applying an early mono sum. The delay length is common to Left and Right, because the node models one general source-listener separation rather than calculating a different physical path for each ear.

A distant explosion is a classic example. The visual flash is visible almost immediately, but the sound arrives noticeably later. If the game already knows the distance at the moment of the event, you can latch that value and allow the recording to travel through the buffer. A larger distance should produce a longer wait, without requiring you to write a Blueprint Delay node whose duration you maintain separately.
This is an audio-propagation control, not an attenuation or room model. A real distant explosion may also need appropriate recording perspective, air absorption and environmental effects.

Model changing sound travel time from a moving source, with bounded pitch-like effects and protection against sudden position jumps.

A vehicle approaching and receding changes the distance sound must travel while the recording is playing. Dynamic Propagation accepts a changing Distance (cm) and updates a delay buffer in response. Adjusting playback travel time can create a Doppler-like change in perceived pitch, so the node includes smoothing, a maximum permitted Doppler change and handling for abrupt distance jumps.

This is not the same as merely reducing volume with distance. The node changes the timing of audio samples reaching the listener. The current stereo implementation maintains separate channel delay histories so both recorded channels move through the same propagation model without being summed together.

Imagine an engine recording attached to a fast-moving car. As it approaches, the sound path gets shorter; as it drives away, the path lengthens. The player may hear a controlled movement in pitch and arrival timing. Now teleport the car to a distant location: a naïve delay buffer could click or scrub wildly, which is why jump detection and crossfading are exposed as controls.
Use a fairly constant recording for the first test. If the source contains rapid, unrelated pitch modulation, it is harder to judge whether the propagation effect itself behaves sensibly.

Calculate a pitch multiplier from source and listener motion without rendering audio in the node itself.

The Doppler effect is a change in perceived frequency caused by relative movement along the line between source and listener. Doppler Ratio receives the source's velocity toward the listener and the listener's velocity toward the source, plus the speed of sound. From those controls it produces Pitch Ratio, a Float value suitable for a playback or modulation stage that accepts a linear pitch multiplier.

Unlike Dynamic Propagation, this node does not take In Left or In Right, and it does not output audio. It remains a control-only node despite the broader move to stereo, because a numerical ratio does not have independent audio channels. Changing a control-only node to emit stereo audio would add complexity without making its result more correct.

Picture a horn attached to a train moving toward a stationary listener. The relevant speed is how fast the horn's source is approaching along the listener direction, not merely how fast the train is travelling somewhere on the map. A vehicle driving sideways across the listener's line of sight can have a large total velocity but a much smaller radial velocity.
The same idea applies when the listener is moving. By supplying both toward-velocities you can model which party contributes to the perceived pitch change.

Make distant audio gradually lose some of its high-frequency definition as it travels through air.

Air transmission can change the character of a sound even when no wall or other obstacle exists between source and listener. Atmosphere Absorption uses travelled distance together with temperature, humidity and pressure to estimate frequency-dependent losses. The audible goal is a controlled reduction in brightness as the path grows longer, rather than simply moving the volume slider down.

The stereo version accepts In Left and In Right and produces Out Left and Out Right. Each channel is processed using its own audio history while the environmental controls remain shared. That means stereo ambience or an authored wide sound can retain its left/right differences through the frequency shaping.

Try a short crisp impact or a mechanical sound with noticeable high-frequency content. Compare a near distance with a much larger one, leaving the Wave Asset unchanged. At a longer path, you should expect the very bright content to be less pronounced. You can then adjust the atmospheric conditions and hear how the approximate absorption model responds.

In a game, this effect can complement distance-recording choices. A distant weapon tail is not just a close gunshot made quieter, so use appropriate source material as well as DSP when the perspective change matters.
